storyboard.claim: Cold open: Johann Hari threw the phone away and still could not escape what it had done.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johann in a wooden cabin on a grey winter shore, low waves dragging behind him; one phone lies face-down on the step beside his boot, untouched, and he is looking past it at the empty water.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Nothing yet — this is the first frame, the failed detox before any analysis.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the three months and the sea live in the audio; the picture only has a cabin, a cold ocean and a phone left behind.

storyboard.claim: Three months without a phone did not buy back one chapter — the damage is not the device.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same cabin table: a book open face-down with the pen beside it, no bookmark moved, no page turned; Johann holds it in both hands and has stopped trying, shoulders down, eyes on nothing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question beat 0 raised: the escape was real and it did not work.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the absence, not the reading — the untouched book is the failure; the staged contrast is the open book and the closed eyes.

storyboard.claim: This is Johann Hari, the journalist behind Stolen Focus, and he is taking his godson Adam to Elvis's estate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johann in a navy blazer holding his own book out at chest height, free arm pointing south down the road; Adam, lanky in a red t-shirt, slouches beside him with his hands in his pockets, unconvinced.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the man who failed in the cabin and introduces the trip that explains him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the book's own title on screen and establishes that Johann and Adam travel together, which the next beats depend on.

storyboard.claim: As a small boy Adam was completely absorbed by Elvis — singing, running, fully present.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boy in a red t-shirt dancing in front of a television with his mouth open mid-song and both fists in the air; beside him, Elvis in the white beaded jumpsuit and pompadour, microphone up, mid-performance on the screen and in the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The Elvis obsession is the bond that gets the two of them into a car to Graceland.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two figures are deliberately unlike each other — a small boy in a red t-shirt against a man in a white beaded jumpsuit — so the picture reads as obsession, not as two similar men.

storyboard.claim: Adam is a teenager now, and his attention has come apart.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split frame: on the left the same boy still singing with his whole body; on the right the same boy as a lanky teenager, folded over a sofa with three separate screens glowing around him, his head pulled three different ways, his face blank and tired.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly opposite beat 3 — same boy, same love of Elvis, opposite state.
storyboard.addedInformation: A fracture has no drawable icon, so the split carries it: the before and the after of one body. No icon is safer here than a wrong one.

storyboard.claim: He cannot stay on one subject and he is always reaching for a screen — so Johann decides to change the scenery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adam's hand already diving into his jeans pocket for the phone; beside him Johann watches, jaw tight, the decision arriving on his face as he looks away down the road.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the abstract fracture of beat 4 into a habit, and hands the problem to Johann.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reach toward the pocket makes the need physical and involuntary — it is not a choice he is making.

callout.text: CHANGE THE SCENERY TO RESET OUR BRAINS

storyboard.claim: Johann's plan is the natural instinct most of us share: change the scenery and the brain resets.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Front seats of a car on an empty open road; Johann's arm out the window, finger pointing at the country going by, while Adam finally looks out of the window instead of at a screen.
storyboard.onScreenText: CHANGE THE SCENERY TO RESET OUR BRAINS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Executes the plan formed in beat 5, and names the assumption the book is about to break.
storyboard.addedInformation: The road is the one object that literally is a change of scenery, and Adam's eyes leaving the screen is the hope the narration is quoting before it is dismantled.

storyboard.claim: They arrive at Graceland and the physical reality is intercepted before they get a single step into it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The front of a grand white-columned Memphis house; at the entrance a lit display case is handing a glowing tablet to every visitor, Johann taking his, Adam's face turned past it to the house itself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The scenery change of beat 6 is answered at the gate — the world they came for is filtered before entry.
storyboard.addedInformation: No icon reads as interception, so the picture does the work: a hand pushing a screen into the visitor's hands at the door.

storyboard.claim: No human guide meets them; the doorway hands every visitor a tablet and headphones instead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The entry arch with nobody manning it; Johann stands holding a tablet and a pair of headphones, glancing up at the empty arch where a guide should be. Behind him a visitor has the headphones on already and his face is down into the screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism beat 7 only implied: the interception is a distribution desk at the door.
storyboard.addedInformation: The absent guide is staged as an absence — an arch with no person in it — rather than by showing a guide.

storyboard.claim: They walk into the Jungle Room, Elvis's favourite place: green shag on the ceiling and a built-in rock waterfall.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The camera looks up into the room: green shag carpet across the ceiling, a carved rock waterfall down the wall. Johann and Adam stand below it with their chins up, Johann's finger pointing at the ceiling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The interior they were promised at the door, and the thing that will lose to the tablets.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the shag and the waterfall are described in the audio; the picture's job is to put a remarkable room in front of the viewer before the next beat ignores it.

storyboard.claim: The room is right there begging to be looked at, and every single person in it is staring at a tablet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A visitor in a wrinkled chambray shirt, face washed blue by his tablet, elbow nudging the woman beside him; across the room Johann has turned and is watching them, with the real waterfall behind his own back.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The first evidence that the room loses — Johann catches it happening.
storyboard.addedInformation: Johann's back is to the waterfall while the man faces it, so the frame shows the crowd choosing the screen over the thing in front of them.

callout.text: SWIPING FOR A PHOTO OF THE ROOM

storyboard.claim: A man swipes on a screen to see a picture of the left side of the room they are standing in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close on the man's hands and face: one thumb swiping left across a tablet showing a flat digital image of the green shag room; a few feet behind his shoulder the real waterfall runs, unremarked.
storyboard.onScreenText: SWIPING FOR A PHOTO OF THE ROOM
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The exact version of beat 10, close enough to touch: the simulation beating the reality it photographs.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two layers in one frame — thumb and tablet in front, waterfall behind the shoulder — is the whole argument of the beat, silent.

callout.text: HIDING HIS PHONE UNDER HIS JACKET

storyboard.claim: The boy who loved Elvis most is hiding his phone inside his jacket to check it without being caught.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adam hunched over, one hand slipped inside his jacket, a strip of screen light leaking out of the gap; his eyes flick sideways to Johann, who has just turned and is looking straight at him.
storyboard.onScreenText: HIDING HIS PHONE UNDER HIS JACKET
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the crowd's absorption personal: the one person the trip was for is the worst offender.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phone is not in his hand — the light leaking from under the jacket is the tell, and Johann's caught look is why he is frantic.

callout.text: NOT A SIGN OF WEAK WILLPOWER

storyboard.claim: Failing to focus is not weak personal willpower — and Johann sees that in the room, not in an argument.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johann's face is steady and un-blaming, open palm turned outward toward a slumped visitor clutching a phone; the visitor is the one who looks bad, and Johann is the one offering his hand, not pointing a finger.
storyboard.onScreenText: NOT A SIGN OF WEAK WILLPOWER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The realisation beat 12 forces: the boy's behaviour is the system's output, not a character flaw.
storyboard.addedInformation: Staged as the contrast, not the failure: no contempt, no scolding — the open palm and the other man's slump carry the negation.

callout.text: DESIGNED TO PROFIT OFF EVERY GLANCE

storyboard.claim: It is the result of an economy designed to profit from every single glance you take away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator alone in a hard pool of light, thumb and forefinger aimed at a bullseye; where her finger points, a pair of eyes is turned away from a screen — the glance is the thing being aimed at.
storyboard.onScreenText: DESIGNED TO PROFIT OFF EVERY GLANCE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pivot of the piece: the culprit is designed, not personal.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target is drawn as the aim itself — the narrator's finger, the bullseye, the eyes off-screen — so the icon reads as aiming at a glance rather than as achievement.

storyboard.claim: The show announces the turn: attention has to be re-modelled, not just tried harder at.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator at the front of a bare stage, one hand sweeping the old model off the air and the other opening toward the viewer; nothing else is on the set.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Handing the analysis over from the Graceland story to the deep dive.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks this as the hosts' analysis, which is why the host and not the reporter is on screen.

storyboard.claim: We all think of attention as a personal resource we produce, like sweat when we exercise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator standing very still, both hands pressed flat together at her waist as if squeezing something out of them; she is turning the old model over in her head while she names it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the wrong model the hosts are about to replace.
storyboard.addedInformation: The squeezing hands stage the sweat metaphor physically; no icon does, and a coin here would read as money and endorse it.

storyboard.claim: The reality is that attention is a common — a free river that flows and belongs to all of us.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wide band of clear running water across the frame, unbroken and unhurried; the narrator stands at its edge with both hands open, palms up, taking none of it for herself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Replaces the sweating-athlete model with the shared river that carries the rest of the act.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator takes nothing from the water: an open hand, not a cup or a tap, so the common is visible before anyone steals from it.

storyboard.claim: Over the past few decades that river has been fenced off and dammed up by massive corporations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same water, now behind a fence running the full width of the frame; the narrator has both hands on it, shaking it, the flow piling up dammed on the far side.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the free river of beat 17 into the fenced one — the theft begins here.
storyboard.addedInformation: The fence is drawn across the water itself, so the icon reads as bound and shut rather than as a link or a chain of history.

callout.text: BOTTLED AND SOLD AS LIKES AND ADS

storyboard.claim: They polluted it, then bottled the water and sold it back to you a glass at a time as likes, notifications and ads.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An exhausted worker holds a phone at arm's length; on the screen a single drop of water is poured into a bottle, and beside the bottle a coin drops into a slot to pay for it.
storyboard.onScreenText: BOTTLED AND SOLD AS LIKES AND ADS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the river arc: fenced, then bottled, then sold back with a price tag.
storyboard.addedInformation: The coin is a payment at a slot, not a reward in a hand — the transaction is the claim, and the worker's tired face keeps it from reading as an endorsement of money.

storyboard.claim: Because it is a systemic theft, the only way to get attention back is collective — and now the hosts ask how the river was dammed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator standing with one hand on her hip and the other flat, palm down, pressing the question into the air in front of her; the fence and the water are behind her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Rules out the lone lifhack before the mechanism-by-mechanism investigation starts.
storyboard.addedInformation: The key is the one thing on screen that suggests getting in; it points forward to the structural answer instead of back at willpower.

storyboard.claim: It was not one big wall — it was a series of structural changes to how we live and how we work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator at the edge of the frame with both hands out to either side, splitting one thing into two; behind her an ordinary office and an ordinary home, side by side.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers beat 20's question by turning the theft into a list of ordinary places, not a single villain.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two buckets are the narrator's own words, so the diagram shows the investigation's map before the first mechanism is named.

storyboard.claim: The first major mechanism of the theft is staged in the harsh clinical light of a Target store in Boston.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johann walking a wide big-box aisle under hard white fluorescent tubes, flat tall shelves closing in on both sides, a basket in his hand, the light flat and unkind on his face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the diagram's 'how we work' bucket into one specific, checkable place.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the brand and the city are words; what the frame adds is the light — clinical, even, designed to keep a person moving down the aisle.

storyboard.claim: Preparing his Provincetown detox, Johann decides he needs one phone, and it is to be a basic one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johann stopped in the middle of a cold coastal street with a box in the other hand, turning a phone over and over in his palm, deciding.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Prepares the detox that failed in beat 0 and the purchase that goes wrong in the next beats.
storyboard.addedInformation: The turning-over hand is the deliberation; the box beside him says he is already packed for the cabin.

storyboard.claim: He asks for the cheapest, most basic phone in the shop — one that explicitly cannot connect to the internet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Over Johann's shoulder: the electronics counter, a wall of identical glowing smartphones behind glass, and on the far side a clerk staring at him with his mouth slightly open and one hand frozen mid-reach.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The request that makes the clerk's bafflement inevitable.
storyboard.addedInformation: The wall of identical lit screens behind the clerk is the thing being refused: Johann asks her to step outside it.

storyboard.claim: The clerk cannot compute the request and keeps warning him, as if no internet were a defect.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close on the clerk: brow up, genuinely troubled, one small phone pushed out in a warning gesture while the other hand is already reaching for the next one on the shelf.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The clerk's objection, delivered as sincere concern rather than a sales pitch.
storyboard.addedInformation: Staged as one person only, so the viewer sees the real face of the assumption instead of two similar salesmen.

storyboard.claim: He is not upselling — he genuinely cannot fathom why a person would choose to cut off the incoming stream.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same clerk now holds the tiny phone out at arm's length like something he is not sure of, the gesture halfway between a recommendation and a warning; his eyes are on Johann, not the device.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what the clerk cannot imagine, and it is the crack the next beat opens wide.
storyboard.addedInformation: The arm's-length grip shows reluctance without staging a villain; the wrongness is in his face, not in his hands.

storyboard.claim: Choosing to disconnect, and to focus on a single thing, has become entirely alien.
storyboard.concreteVisual: One desk under one lamp with one open book on it; the narrator stands just outside the pool of light pointing at it, everything else in the room dark and switched off.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The clerk's bafflement becomes a statement about all of us.
storyboard.addedInformation: The single lit object is the picture of the thing nobody in the story can imagine doing on purpose.

storyboard.claim: This exposes a societywide delusion we have all bought into: the myth of multitasking.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator at the desk with one finger raised; behind her three tasks run at once on three screens, each one stopped halfway and none of them finished.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the delusion the disconnected phone exposed, before they take it apart.
storyboard.addedInformation: The myth is staged mid-performance rather than at rest, so the viewer sees three things going nowhere at once.

storyboard.claim: We convinced ourselves we can do five things at once and do them all well; in truth multitasking is a con and it charges a switching tax.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker with a phone in one hand and the keyboard under the other, head snapping back and forth; the half-typed email on the monitor has not gained a single word.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on the myth from beat 28, and the first cost the book puts a number on.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stalled email is the evidence: whatever the hands are doing, the work is not moving.

storyboard.claim: The word was never applied to people: multitasking is a computing term invented in the 1960s.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator has turned to point at something off-frame as if checking a fact; her other hand is up, palm out, stilling the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The switch that taxes us, beat 29, turns out to be borrowed vocabulary.
storyboard.addedInformation: The correction is dated and named here, which is the information the narration is about to make concrete with a diagram.

storyboard.claim: A term coined for machines with multiple processors was applied to our own neurobiology, blindly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator stands at the end of a chain she is drawing in the air with one finger — a label, then a machine, then a human head; her finger comes to rest on the head.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the borrowing beat 30 set up: the term's journey from chip to person.
storyboard.addedInformation: The three labels are the narrator's own nouns in order, so the chain shows where the word came from before the video explains what it costs.

callout.text: ONE OR TWO THOUGHTS AT A TIME

storyboard.claim: The conscious mind — the part that thinks, reasons and writes — can only produce one or two thoughts at a time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A desk with a single lit page of handwriting in front of the worker; every other screen behind him is dark and silent, and he is only looking at one of them.
storyboard.onScreenText: ONE OR TWO THOUGHTS AT A TIME
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hardware limit behind the switching tax, said plainly before the data.
storyboard.addedInformation: One lit page among dark screens shows the limit as a capacity, not as an opinion.

storyboard.claim: That is a hard neurological limit, and the data on how hard we try to break it is staggering.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator leans in over a working desk with a stopwatch in her hand, counting; behind her a wall of clocks, none of them agreeing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the single-lit-page picture into evidence, and hands the counting to a researcher.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the staggering size of the data is a number in the audio; the frame's job is to look like measurement, which is what the next beat delivers in person.

storyboard.claim: Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at UC Irvine, has spent years studying how people behave in modern offices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gloria in a forest-green cardigan with her notebook open in one hand, standing just inside a working office, watching a desk the way someone watches a lab — patiently, pen still down.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the person behind the data of beat 33.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her name and field are on screen, spelled right, and her unraised pen shows the method starting before she explains it.

storyboard.claim: She did not ask people how they felt; she went into offices with a stopwatch and timed everything they did.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gloria in the aisle with a stopwatch raised at head height, timing a man at his desk; her notebook is tucked under her elbow, already filling up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The method itself — measurement instead of self-report.
storyboard.addedInformation: The raised stopwatch is the object the claim is about, and the untouched-by-him man being timed is the ordinary worker, not a laboratory subject.

storyboard.claim: The average office worker is interrupted every three minutes — a Slack ping, an email chime, a hand on the shoulder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A phone face-up on a desk mid-buzz while a colleague's hand lands on the worker's shoulder at the same instant; his pen has stopped on the word it was writing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gloria's stopwatch produces its first number, and it is a very small number.
storyboard.addedInformation: Both causes arrive in one frame at once, which is what makes the three minutes feel like a pattern instead of an accident.

callout.text: NO FULL HOUR OF UNBROKEN WORK

storyboard.claim: Most office workers never get one uninterrupted hour in a whole day, and we pay a physical and mental price for that.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gloria has looked down at her stopwatch, disbelieving, then up at a worker with his head in both hands; behind them a clock face and a door that keeps swinging open.
storyboard.onScreenText: NO FULL HOUR OF UNBROKEN WORK
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The second, more terrible metric — and the handoff to the neuroscientist who explains the price.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her disbelieving face carries the horror in the number; the worker with his head in his hands carries the price the narration mentions at the end of the beat.

callout.text: WRITING AN EMAIL WHEN THE PHONE BUZZES

storyboard.claim: Earl Miller of MIT mapped what happens inside the brain when you multitask; here is the case: an important email and a text arriving.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Earl Miller in a tweed jacket with one finger raised to make a point; beside him at a desk a worker types a serious email, a phone lying face-up a few inches from the keyboard.
storyboard.onScreenText: WRITING AN EMAIL WHEN THE PHONE BUZZES
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings on the neuroscientist whose evidence the last beat promised, and sets up the experiment.
storyboard.addedInformation: The email and the phone share one desk an inch apart, so the next beats can measure the distance the head has to travel.

storyboard.claim: You glance down at the text and straight back up to keep typing, and to you it costs nothing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close on the worker's eyes: down to the lit phone and straight back up to the screen — a flicker and no change in his face, no time visibly lost.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The ordinary case from beat 38, at the moment it feels free; the price arrives in the next beats.
storyboard.addedInformation: The untroubled face is the point: the cost is real but invisible, so the picture must not show pain here.
